channel.title: MIA — Management Intelligence Alert
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: The World Bank projects output in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan to contract by 2.1% in 2026 after 3.3% growth in 2025, with GCC economies contracting by an average 4.3%, citing the conflict that began in February.
item.description:
Oil-importing countries in the region have remained comparatively resilient, with growth projected to rise to 4.3% in 2026 from 3.9% in 2025, The Nation reports. In April the Bank had projected growth of 1.8% for the region's economies excluding Iran and 1.3% for the GCC, and growth expectations for the region have been revised down by about 3.9 percentage points from the April forecast, Asharq Al-Awsat reports on the update titled "From Divide to Opportunity: AI, Jobs, and Growth". For 2027 the Bank projects GCC growth of 10.3% if the conflict does not escalate in 2026, on the assumption that oil production and shipping return to normal from early 2027, and growth of 7.8% for the region excluding Iran, driven mainly by recovering hydrocarbon production and exports, Arab News reports. The reporting does not make clear whether the 2.1% contraction includes Iran, so the 3.9-point revision may compare different country groups, and it does not give country figures.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The figures are forecasts, and the 2027 rebound is explicitly conditional on shipping and oil production normalising. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a contraction concentrated in the oil exporters reflects lost hydrocarbon output and exports rather than weaker demand elsewhere in the region. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, the Gulf is both a construction market and a supplier of petrochemical raw materials, so the recovery path matters on the demand side and on the supply side. Points that may be worth considering include whether shipping through the region normalises on the assumed timetable, and how Gulf construction programmes are affected in 2026.

The Nation | Asharq Al-Awsat | Arab News

item.title: Vietnam's GDP grew 9.95% year on year in the third quarter of 2026, after 8.15% in the first quarter and 8.81% in the second, with industry and construction expanding 11.21% over nine months, official data show.
item.description:
The figures come from the National Statistics Office under the Ministry of Finance, Vietnam Economic Times reports. In the first nine months, industry and construction contributed nearly half of total value added, while services grew 8.69% and agriculture, forestry and fisheries 4.02%. Over the same nine months, registered foreign investment rose 76.4% from a year earlier to USD 50.36 billion and disbursed foreign direct investment 12.1% to USD 21.07 billion, Vietnam News.Net reports; manufacturing and processing took 45.8%, or USD 13.38 billion, of newly registered capital, and Singapore was the largest source. Separately, Dünya reports that the "China Plus One" strategy has not yielded the expected outcome, that factories in Southeast Asia still depend on China for critical parts, and that some computer manufacturers are moving from Vietnam and Thailand back to China. The reporting does not give the nine-month GDP growth rate or the export figures.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

GDP growth, registered investment and disbursed investment are different measures; registered and disbursed figures differ, at USD 50.36 billion and USD 21.07 billion. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, growth led by industry and construction, with foreign investment concentrated in manufacturing, points to Vietnam's continued role as an assembly base, while Dünya reports that factories in Southeast Asia still depend on China for critical parts. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, Vietnam's electronics, footwear, furniture and construction sectors are bonding-intensive users whose demand follows this growth. Points that may be worth considering include whether disbursement catches up with registered investment, and how much of the parts supply is localised.

Vietnam Economic Times | Vietnam News.Net | Dünya Gazetesi

item.title: Extreme weather and climate events destroyed or damaged EUR 822bn of assets in the EU between 1980 and 2024, in 2024 prices, with EUR 208bn lost in 2021–2024 alone, according to the European indicator reported by La Tribune.
item.description:
Average annual losses rose from EUR 19.7bn in the 2010s to EUR 44.9bn over 2020–2024, La Tribune reports. The EUR 208bn lost in 2021–2024 is a quarter of the 45-year total. Floods account for 47% of cumulative damage since 1980, far ahead of storms at 27% and heatwaves at almost 18%. The indicator counts direct damage to buildings, equipment and infrastructure; it leaves out interrupted activity, lower productivity, healthcare expenses, lost tax revenues and the cost of more resilient reconstruction. The reporting does not give the breakdown by country, the insured share of the losses, or the 2025 figure.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The figures are historical and cover direct damage only, and the indicator leaves out interrupted activity, lost productivity and other indirect costs. On a general reading rather than on anything in the source, losses concentrated in floods and storms translate into repair and reconstruction of buildings and infrastructure, and into pressure for more resilient construction standards. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, that reaches renovation demand and the requirements placed on sealing, waterproofing and moisture-resistant bonding in buildings. Points that may be worth considering include whether EU or national building rules respond with resilience requirements, how insurers price flood risk, and whether the 2025 figure continues the trend.

La Tribune

item.title: A study by economists at the German Economic Institute (IW), co-financed by the Federal Foreign Office, says large direct investments by German companies in China and dependencies on China threaten Germany's sovereignty and German taxpayers, FAZ reports.
item.description:
To reduce the risks, the economists demand from the federal government a clear signal that German taxpayers would not bail out German companies for possible major losses of their subsidiaries in China in a geopolitical conflict, Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung reports. The economists also call on the government to opt clearly for value creation and employment in Germany in conflicts of interest between German companies operating in China and Germany as a location, and to prevent excessive incentives for relocating activities to China. FAZ describes the IW as employer-friendly and notes that the study comes as the European Union discusses new trade policy instruments against China. The reporting does not give the size of German direct investment in China, the companies or sectors most exposed, how the risk to taxpayers is quantified, or the government's response.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The study makes recommendations; it is not a policy decision and the government's position is not reported. On a general reading rather than on anything in the source, a stated refusal to cover losses in a geopolitical conflict would move the risk of China exposure from the state to the investing company, which tends to raise the return that companies require from new investment there. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, German producers that serve Chinese customers from local plants would weigh that risk against the advantage of producing close to the customer. Points that may be worth considering include whether the federal government adopts any of the recommendations, whether the government signals that it would not cover losses of China subsidiaries, and how the study is used in the EU discussion on new trade instruments.

Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung

item.title: Becton Dickinson has signed a deal with the US government to invest USD 19 billion in the US over several years, in return for relief from future Section 232 tariffs, subject to the final scope of the measures and agreed milestones.
item.description:
The company will direct USD 3 billion of the total to manufacturing expansion at strategic US sites, within a total that includes capital, operational and supply-chain investments, according to the company and MarketScreener. It plans to produce an additional 5 billion medical consumables a year in the US, which it says would raise its share of domestically supplied essential medical consumables to around 80%, and to make all of its needles used in the US domestically from American-made steel. The tariff relief is subject to the final scope of the measures and to the company meeting agreed milestones. The deal follows the administration's push to use tariff threats to spur domestic healthcare manufacturing, with major drugmakers already pledging billions for new and expanded US production and research facilities. The reporting does not give which products are covered, the tariff rates avoided, the timetable, or where the added production currently comes from.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

This is one company's agreement; it follows the administration's push to use tariff threats to spur domestic healthcare manufacturing, under which major drugmakers have already pledged billions for US production and research facilities. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, such deals move production of covered goods into the US and tie it to US-made inputs, as the needle-steel commitment shows, which can shift demand for components and materials to US suppliers. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, medical device and consumables assembly uses bonding and coating materials, so relocated production changes where those materials are qualified and bought. Points that may be worth considering include the final scope of the Section 232 measures on medical products, whether other medical technology companies sign similar deals, and whether the input commitments extend beyond steel.

MarketScreener | MarketScreener | MarketScreener

item.title: A new IEA report finds Southeast Asia is using more energy than ever but becoming increasingly reliant on imported fuel, with electricity demand expected to grow about 5.4% a year in 2026–2030.
item.description:
Before 28 February, when the United States and Israel launched strikes on Iran, about 60% of Southeast Asia's crude oil imports and one-third of its natural gas imports came from the Middle East, CNA reports. That expected growth is driven by industrial expansion, cooling needs and the rapid development of data centres, CNA reports. The report, released on 6 October, says energy supply risks are growing rapidly, far outpacing the speed at which countries are proposing solutions to meet electricity demand, Chinatimes.com reports. The IEA urged the region to diversify energy sources and supply routes, use domestic resources where viable and expand efficiency and electrification, CNA reports, and the report recommends sharing electricity across borders, according to Chinatimes.com and the South China Morning Post; analysts quoted by the South China Morning Post warn that differing national energy markets and territorial disputes may keep the region vulnerable. Separately, Southeast Asian energy ministers are meeting in Manila to discuss regional fuel-security measures, and the ASEAN Centre for Energy warns that a severe Middle East disruption could put oil volumes equivalent to nearly 28% of ASEAN's final oil consumption at risk, MarketScreener reports. The reporting does not give country figures or price projections.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The report is an assessment of exposure and demand, not a measured supply disruption; the 60% import share and the 28% at-risk volume are different measures on different bases and are not combined here. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a manufacturing region that imports most of its crude and a growing share of its energy carries that dependence into factory energy costs and supply reliability. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, production and customers in Thailand, Vietnam, Indonesia and Malaysia are exposed to the same fuel and power costs, both directly and through local petrochemical supply. Points that may be worth considering include the outcome of the ministers' meeting, progress on cross-border power trade, and whether fuel-security measures under the ASEAN petroleum framework are activated.

CNA | Chinatimes.com | South China Morning Post | MarketScreener

item.title: The German government's new economic forecast predicts GDP growth of 1.3% this year and 1.1% next year, with exports up 3.7% and 2.1%, according to Handelsblatt information; Chancellor Merz discussed it with the heads of business associations.
item.description:
Merz met the presidents and chief executives of the German Chamber of Industry and Commerce (DIHK), the German Confederation of Skilled Crafts (ZDH), the Federation of German Industries (BDI) and the Confederation of German Employers' Associations (BDA) to discuss the forecast, Handelsblatt reports. According to the paper, exports are doing surprisingly well, and high government spending on defence and infrastructure is driving the upswing. The figures are reported on the basis of Handelsblatt information; the reporting does not say whether the forecast has been published. The reporting does not give the government's previous forecast, so the size of any revision is not known; it also does not give the assumptions for inflation, employment, investment or energy prices, the breakdown by sector, or whether and when the forecast is published.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The figures are a government forecast reported according to Handelsblatt information, not measured output. On a general reading rather than on anything in the source, growth driven by public spending on defence and infrastructure reaches industry through public construction, civil engineering and defence manufacturing rather than through private consumption or private investment. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, demand in the home market would then depend more on infrastructure and public building programmes and on defence-related manufacturing than on housing or consumer goods. Points that may be worth considering include the published forecast and its comparison with the government's previous forecast, how much of the growth the government attributes to public spending, and the export assumptions behind the 3.7% and 2.1% figures.

Handelsblatt

item.title: Electric vehicles made up around 13% of India's 2.537 million vehicle registrations in September 2026, according to FADA data, with registrations of electric cars and SUVs nearly doubling from a year earlier to around 36,100.
item.description:
Electric two-wheelers supplied over 60% of EV volumes, The Hindu Business Line reports on FADA data. Electric two-wheeler penetration rose to 11.58% in September from 8.17% a year earlier, as registrations nearly doubled to around 207,000. Three-wheelers remained the most electrified category, with the EV share at 64.9% against 56.65% a year earlier, around 86,000 units against around 61,400. In passenger vehicles, EV penetration rose to 8.45% from 5.74%, around 36,100 electric cars and SUVs against 18,600 a year earlier. The reporting does not give the change in total registrations from a year earlier, the total for passenger vehicles, or the policy measures behind the shift.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The figures are registrations and shares in one month; the overall year-earlier total is not given, so the change in the whole market is not known, although EV volumes rose in each segment reported. On a general reading rather than on anything in the source, electric drivetrains change the bill of materials of a vehicle, with battery packs, motors and power electronics replacing parts of the combustion powertrain, and in India this shift is led by two- and three-wheelers rather than cars. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, the change matters for bonding, sealing and thermal-management materials in battery and vehicle assembly, which differ from those used in combustion vehicles. Points that may be worth considering include the total market trend, where in India the batteries are assembled, and whether passenger-car penetration keeps rising at this pace.

The Hindu Business Line

item.title: New orders in German industry fell 10.6% in August 2026 from July, the strongest decline since the start of the year, Federal Statistical Office data show, while excluding large orders they were 0.1% lower than in July.
item.description:
The overall decline is entirely attributable to a 61.5% fall in what the statistics office classifies as "other transport equipment", MarketScreener reports; Chinatimes.com reports that this category had more than doubled in July because of an unusually high number of large orders. Handelsblatt reports that the decline is attributed to the loss of large defence orders and notes that the category includes aircraft, ships, trains and military vehicles. Domestic orders fell 17.3% from July and foreign orders 5.4%, with orders from the euro zone down 5.4% and from outside the euro zone down 5.5%. In the less volatile three-month comparison, new orders from June to August were 1.3% higher than in the previous three months. The reporting does not give the change in orders for chemicals, motor vehicles, machinery or electrical equipment, the year-on-year change, or the change in industrial production.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The headline fall is driven by one category after an exceptional July; excluding large orders the month was nearly flat, and the three-month comparison is positive, so the three measures describe different things rather than one trend. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, large defence and transport orders arrive in lumps and are delivered over years, so they move monthly orders far more than the underlying flow of business. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, the German industrial customer base in vehicles, machinery and electrical equipment is better read through the orders excluding large contracts than through the headline. Points that may be worth considering include the September orders data, whether domestic orders excluding large contracts weaken, and the breakdown by industry.

Handelsblatt | MarketScreener | Chinatimes.com

item.title: The S&P Global UK construction PMI reached 46.1 in September 2026, the sector's strongest performance for eight months and the slowest rate of decline since January, with house building the weakest category.
item.description:
The figures were released by S&P Global Market Intelligence, The Independent reports. S&P noted that house building was the weakest performer, as unfavourable market conditions and rising borrowing costs weighed on output. The index therefore still describes a decline in construction activity in September, but one that was slower than in any month since January. The reporting does not give the August reading, the indices for commercial building and civil engineering, new orders, employment, input prices, or what S&P expects for the coming months. It rests on one source.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The 46.1 reading marks the slowest rate of decline since January, not a return to growth. On a general reading rather than on anything in the source, borrowing costs bear most directly on house building, which tends to make residential work the last part of construction to turn when rates are rising. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, UK demand for construction adhesives, sealants and flooring products follows construction activity, with residential work — the weakest category here — a large share of that demand. Points that may be worth considering include whether the index moves above 50 in the coming months, how the house-building index compares with commercial and civil engineering, and how UK borrowing costs develop.

The Independent

item.title: DIC and the artience Group, through its packaging subsidiary Toyo Ink, have established what they call the industry's first common protocol for testing deinking and delamination in the material recycling of film packaging in Japan.
item.description:
The protocol standardises test procedures, evaluation criteria and reporting formats for deinking and delamination in the material recycling of film packaging within the Japanese market, MarketScreener reports. MarketScreener reports that it provides stakeholders across the supply chain, including converters, brand owners and recyclers, a unified environment in which to evaluate and compare recyclability on shared domestic standards. The reporting does not give which film structures or ink and adhesive systems the protocol covers, the pass criteria, when it takes effect, whether other suppliers, converters or recyclers have joined, or whether it is linked to any Japanese regulation or to test methods used outside Japan. It rests on one source, MarketScreener's report of the companies' announcement.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The protocol is a shared evaluation method announced by two companies, not a regulation. On a general reading rather than on anything in the source, a common test makes the recyclability of a laminate comparable between suppliers, which tends to turn how easily a package separates into a specification that converters and brand owners can ask for. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, laminating adhesives, primers and inks are the layers such a test examines, so a supplier-led protocol can become a reference point for what a recyclable flexible laminate means in Japan. Points that may be worth considering include whether converters, brand owners and recyclers adopt the protocol, whether it is referenced by Japanese packaging rules, and whether comparable protocols appear in Europe or other Asian markets.

MarketScreener

item.title: President Trump signed an executive order on 5 October to temporarily ease limits on tax-exempt dyed diesel, directing the Treasury and defence secretaries to suspend the federal excise tax on dyed diesel used on highways for the rest of the year.
item.description:
Dyed, or "red", diesel is exempt from the 24-cent-a-gallon federal diesel tax and is generally reserved for off-road use on farms and construction sites, The Financial Times reports. The order also directs the two secretaries to "explore pathways" to scrap any obligations to pay the deferred taxes, instructs the transportation and agriculture secretaries to co-ordinate access to dyed diesel, in particular by farmers, and to encourage states to take similar steps to suspend their own duties. Lianhe Zaobao reports that the order allows dyed diesel, previously limited to off-road uses such as agriculture and construction, to be purchased by all users, and that wider use in road vehicles without penalty may mean substantial tax relief in some cases. The reporting does not give the reason stated for the order, its estimated cost to federal revenue, whether supply of dyed diesel is sufficient for wider road use, how much of the saving is expected to reach pump prices, or how the deferred-tax question will be settled.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The order directs a suspension of the 24-cent-a-gallon federal tax on dyed diesel used on highways for the rest of the year, with the deferred-tax obligations still to be settled; it is not a price series, and the effect on what users pay depends on pass-through, which the reporting does not give. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, lower road-fuel tax reduces the cost of trucking and other road transport in the US, while off-road machinery already runs on tax-exempt dyed diesel and the open question of deferred taxes leaves the final size of the relief uncertain. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, the effect would show mainly in US distribution and freight costs rather than in raw-material prices. Points that may be worth considering include whether states suspend their own duties, whether the deferred taxes are scrapped, and whether the measure is extended beyond the year.

The Financial Times | Lianhe Zaobao
